cheatsheet:
**Every program**
`#include <stdio.h>` at the top, then `int main(void) { ... return 0; }`. The computer starts at `main`.

**Printing**
`printf("text\n");` prints text. Every statement ends with `;`.

**Escapes inside quotes**
`\n` new line · `\t` tab · `\"` a quote mark · `\\` a backslash

**Comments**
`// to the end of the line` and `/* across lines */`. The compiler ignores both.

**When it won't compile**
Read the first error only. The line number is usually right, or one line below the real mistake.

lessons.title: Hello, station
lessons.concept:
A program is a list of instructions the computer follows **top to bottom**.

In C, it always starts at `main`. Everything between `main`'s `{` and `}` runs in order.

`printf` prints text. The text goes inside quotes, and `\n` means "new line". Each instruction ends with `;`, like a full stop.

The first line, `#include <stdio.h>`, brings in `printf`. Without it, C doesn't know what printing is.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: what will this program print?
predict.explain: Only the text inside the quotes is printed. `\n` isn't shown: it moves to a new line.

drills.prompt: Fill in the two missing words so this program compiles.
drills.explain: `stdio.h` brings in `printf`, and every program starts at `main`.
Without `\n`, the next printf carries on on the same line. So `A` and `B` end up side by side.

drills.prompt: Put the lines in order, with the right indents, to make a working program.
drills.explain: Include first, then `main` opens with `{`, the instructions go inside (indented), and `}` closes it.

lessons.title: New lines and other escapes
lessons.concept:
Some characters can't be typed straight into quotes, so C uses **escapes**: a backslash plus a letter.

`\n` new line · `\t` tab · `\"` a quote mark · `\\` a backslash.

Without `\n`, printf keeps writing on the same line. It never adds a new line for you.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what this prints.
predict.answer:
Line one
Line two
She said "reboot"
predict.explain: A `\n` in the middle of the text breaks the line right there. `\"` prints a real quote mark.

drills.explain: There's a new line after `1`, but none after `2`, so the `3` lands right next to it.
`\t` is a tab: a jump to the next column, handy for lining up readouts.

drills.prompt: This should print `Hull: "OK"` (with the quote marks) but it won't compile. Fix it.
drills.explain: A plain `"` ends the text early. Inside quotes, write `\"` to print a quote mark.

lessons.title: Comments and mistakes
lessons.concept:
**Comments** are notes for humans. The compiler skips them.

`//` hides the rest of a line. `/* ... */` hides everything between, even several lines.

When something won't compile, read the **first** error only. Its line number points at the problem, or the line just after it. A missing `;` is the most common one.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: how many lines does this print?
predict.explain: Only `Fuel check` prints. The note and the old test are comments, so they never run.

drills.explain: `A` and `C` are inside comments. Only `B` and `D` run.

drills.prompt: It should print `Engines: online`. Read the compiler's complaint, then fix it.
drills.explain: Every statement ends with `;`. The compiler noticed when it reached `return` on the next line.

checkpoint.prompt: In `printf("X\tY\n");`, what ends up between X and Y?

checkpoint.explain: The middle printf prints only a new line.

checkpoint.prompt: Order the lines into a working program.
This won't compile. Which line is the problem?
checkpoint.explain: Line 2 is missing its `;`. The compiler may report line 3, because that's where it noticed.
